items.title: Efficient, Elegant, and Environmental Computing
items.text:
We are a computing hardware research group. We study how computing systems can sense, learn, and process information with less energy, while remaining reliable.

Our work connects computer architecture, VLSI design, and neuromorphic computing. We develop software models and FPGA prototypes to investigate the relationship between algorithms, memory, and hardware.

items.title: From ideas to prototypes
items.text:
We investigate architectural trade-offs through modeling, hardware design, and experimental validation. Our projects include FPGA implementations of spiking neural networks, hybrid-memory prototypes, and embedded sensing demonstrations.

Browse our publications for research findings, patents for inventions, and student projects for examples of practical work.

items.title: Life in the group
items.text:
Our students work on software, hardware, and the connections between them. Research involves reading papers, developing and testing ideas, building prototypes, and sharing results through presentations and publications.

Explore our news, events and Open Lab demonstrations, and gallery to see the group's activities. Learn about our approach in How We Work and What You Learn.

We are hiring!

We are looking for motivated Master’s and Ph.D. students and postdoctoral researchers to join our group. Explore our research opportunities and contact us to discuss your interests.

items.title: Research
items.text: We design energy-efficient and reliable computing hardware, from sensing and spike processing to memory architectures and 3D integration. Our work combines architecture design, software models, and FPGA prototyping for edge AI and embedded systems.

items.title: Research areas
items.text:
• Neuromorphic computing: spiking neural networks, approximate computation, and efficient learning and inference.
  • Memory and 3D integration: hybrid memory, stacked architectures, and efficient data movement.
  • Event sensing: asynchronous sensor processing, real-time perception, and low-power embedded implementation.
  • Reliable and sustainable computing: fault tolerance, thermal-aware design, and energy-aware operation.

items.title: Projects and research themes
items.text:
• Low-Power Neuromorphic Computing

    Low-power neuromorphic computing for IoT and edge devices. We investigate approximate neuron circuits and stacked memory to reduce energy use while maintaining accuracy.

    Explore low-power neuromorphic computing

  • HYMEX

    Hybrid non-volatile memory and SRAM for energy-efficient neuromorphic AI. We study 3D memory integration and adaptive power management to reduce operating and idle energy.

    Explore HYMEX

  • Event Sensing

    Efficient processing of asynchronous event-camera data. Our work connects sensing, spiking neural networks, and embedded hardware for real-time perception.

    Explore event sensing

  • 3D-IC Design and Reliability

    Thermal-aware fault detection and recovery for TSV-based 3D networks-on-chip. This project provides foundations for reliable stacked computing systems.

    Explore 3D-IC research

items.title: 低消費電力3Dスタックメモリニューラルネットワークプロセッサ  / Low-Power 3D-Stacked Memory Neural Network Processor
items.text:
ニューラルネットワークをプロセッサに搭載する際、大量のパラメータを格納するために大きなメモリ領域が必要となり、結果として消費電力が大きくなるという課題があります。

When implementing neural networks on-chip, a large memory footprint is required to store the parameters, which leads to increased power consumption.

本研究では、これを解決するために、3Dスタック型の低消費電力ニューラルネットワークプロセッサを提案します。

To address this issue, we propose a low-power 3D-stacked neural network processor.
path: Innovation Japan 2025 – The University Fair ～大学見本市～

items.title: 🔍 主な特徴 / Key Features:
items.text:
• 📦 パラメータを上位・下位ビットに分割してメモリ層に分散配置 / Split parameter storage across upper and lower bits into different memory layers
  • ⚙️ 演算処理を別層に分離し、電圧・電力制御を最適化 / Computation layer isolated from memory for intelligent voltage and power control
  • 🔋 エネルギー効率の高い推論処理を実現（エッジAIや組み込み用途に最適） / Energy-efficient inference processing, ideal for edge and embedded AI applications

この技術は、省電力が求められる次世代AIハードウェアに最適です。現在、事業化や共同研究に向けたパートナーを募集中です。

This technology is designed for next-generation low-power AI hardware, and we are actively seeking collaborators for commercialization and joint research.

  • Description / 説明: 10:00～15:00（休憩12:00～13:00）　@研究棟2F S1

本研究では、低消費電力デバイス上で動作するセンシングシステムの開発を行っています。 展示では、「Raspberry Piとサーマルカメラによる人検出」や「FPGAとイベントカメラによるリアルタイム動体検出」を紹介します。 それぞれ異なる特徴を持つセンサを利用し、環境の変化を高速かつ効率的に検出する技術を体験できます。

This research focuses on developing sensing systems that operate on low-power devices. The exhibition will introduce human detection using a Raspberry Pi and thermal camera, as well as real-time moving-object detection using an FPGA and event camera. Visitors can experience technologies that use different types of sensors to detect environmental changes quickly and efficiently.

items.title: How we work
items.text: We want students to become independent researchers and to feel comfortable asking for help. We work closely together, share progress, and support one another through difficulties. Students' development and well-being guide how we supervise research.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
New students first learn about the group's research, tools, and methods. Ask questions, talk with other students, and explore possible topics.

You will usually begin with a small example project to practise research methods and the programming, data analysis, or experimental work your topic needs. After that, you will join a larger research project with the PI and senior students. As you gain experience, you will take responsibility for part of the work and develop your own ideas.

items.title: Keeping track of the work
items.text:
Each student has a GitHub working repository to record progress. These repositories synchronize with our internal website. We use Slack for group communication and keep meeting logs so that decisions and next steps are recorded.

Students at every level are valued equally. We encourage open communication about progress and problems.

items.title: Supervision and support
items.text:
The PI works with each student according to their strengths, interests, and career plans, with regular feedback. The supervisor is available for discussion most of the time. You can raise research questions as well as academic or personal difficulties; we will listen and help where we can.

We value research results, but helping students become skilled, independent, and considerate researchers comes first. Alongside technical work, we practise writing and presentations, discuss research ethics, and help students build confidence and resilience. These skills matter in academia and in other careers.

items.title: Ideas from the local community
items.text:
We look for ways to apply our research to problems in the community. If you have an idea that could help locally, propose it so we can discuss how to work on it together.

The university's motto, 「地域から世界へ」1, expresses our view that work on local problems can also contribute to research more widely.

items.title: Research and its outcomes
items.text:
Following the university's motto, "to Advance Knowledge for Humanity", we study neuromorphic computing and 3D integrated circuits. Our work includes brain-inspired computing architectures and designs that improve performance, energy efficiency, and integration density.

Students are encouraged to explore these fields and develop their own questions. We publish our findings, including in IEEE Transactions journals, and file and secure patents for inventions developed through the research.

items.title: Writing a research plan
items.text:
Ask for a sample if you are unsure how to begin. Aim for 2-3 pages with clear headings and plain language.

Your proposed work must fit the university's philosophies, 「地域から世界へ」1 and "to Advance Knowledge for Humanity". Read the Japanese admission policy for the university's mission and goals.

items.title: Start with our research
items.text: Read our projects and publications. Identify a topic that interests you, explain how it connects to our work, and say what you would add.

items.title: Explain the problem
items.text: Describe the problem you want to solve, why it matters, and what you hope to achieve. A reader should be able to understand the purpose without already knowing your topic.

items.title: Review existing work
items.text: Summarize the relevant ideas and findings. Explain what remains unresolved and how your project could address it. Mention any local or global problem the research could help with.

items.title: Describe the work you will do
items.text:
Include:

  • Your methods or experiments.
  • The tools and resources you need.
  • Illustrations or diagrams, especially where words alone are difficult to follow.
  • An overall timeline and a detailed schedule with tasks and deadlines.
  • Likely difficulties and how you plan to deal with them.

items.title: Explain the expected contribution
items.text: Say how the work could help the community, industry, or society, and how it fits the university's goals. Mention possible partnerships or collaborations where relevant.

items.title: Revise for clarity
items.text:
Check that each section adds information. Remove unnecessary detail and explain unfamiliar terms. Keep the plan short enough for a reader to understand the problem, approach, and expected contribution in 2-3 pages.

items.title: TA, RA, and part-time work
items.text: If you are concerned about funding your studies, discuss it with us early. We support students who face financial difficulties and are willing to contribute to the lab. Completing a degree can open opportunities for work or further study, but you need a practical plan for your expenses.

items.title: Teaching assistant work
items.text:
Teaching assistants (TAs) help course instructors with grading, tutoring, and administrative tasks. Payment is 20,000 to 40,000 JPY per course, and students can typically take on 3 to 4 courses a year.

TA assignments prioritize courses taught within our lab. You can also ask other professors about opportunities in their courses.

items.title: Research assistant work
items.text:
Research assistants (RAs) contribute to ongoing projects through programming, data analysis, literature review, and experiments. Strong programming skills are essential. We assess students according to their abilities and the needs of the project.

Payment ranges from 10,000 to 70,000 JPY per month, depending on the project and your contribution. RA work depends on project funding and your skills, so we cannot guarantee a position in advance. Developing your technical skills can improve your eligibility.

Doctoral students may receive an additional university RA stipend that typically covers approximately the cost of tuition.

items.title: Other part-time work
items.text: Current and former students have worked part-time for local companies. Ask them about their experience and how to find out more.

items.title: Planning your budget
items.text:
Tuition is approximately 45,000 JPY per month. Living costs are around 50,000 JPY per month if you cook for yourself. All payment and cost figures on this page are in Japanese yen.

Contact us or discuss TA and RA opportunities with the PI if you have questions.

items.title: Experiences of self-financed students
items.text:
The PI completed his Ph.D. as a self-financed student, fully supported by TA and RA work, and went on to an academic career.

A former master's student, Mr. NGUYEN Ngo Doanh, also funded his degree through several TA and RA roles. He published 4 journal papers, including two IEEE Transactions papers, received the Award of Excellence for AY2023, and received a full scholarship for a Ph.D. at a European university.

items.title: What you can learn
items.text: We help students develop the skills to work independently and choose their next steps, whether in research or another career. Our group news includes examples of students' work and achievements.

items.title: Developing your own ideas
items.text: You will practise asking research questions, working through difficult problems, and testing possible solutions. As your project develops, you will take more responsibility for the work and learn to judge which ideas are worth pursuing.

items.title: Writing and presenting
items.text: Research involves explaining your work to other people. You will practise writing papers and reports, making presentations for seminars and conferences, and discussing your ideas. Guidance takes account of how you work and communicate, so you can develop a style that suits you.

items.title: Working with others
items.text: You will work with students and faculty, including people from other disciplines. This gives you practice sharing work, learning from others, and cooperating with people whose knowledge and experience differ from yours.

items.title: Learning with support
items.text: You can discuss research ideas, personal development, and life outside university with us. Supervision depends on your strengths and needs, whether you are learning to approach a research problem or improving a draft or presentation. We want students to leave with the skills and confidence to handle their next project and their next stage in life.

items.title: Event-Driven Low-power Three Dimensional Digital Spiking Neuromorphic System
items.text:
🇬🇧 In this project, students will research and implement an adaptive, low-power spiking neural network system in hardware (NASH) based on our previously developed OASIS communication network. NASH implements the following features (1) efficient adaptive configuration method which enables reconfiguration of different SNN parameters (spike weights, routing, hidden layers, topology, etc.), (2) a mixture of different deep NN topologies, (3) an efficient fault-tolerant multicast spike routing algorithm, (4) Efficient on-chip learning mechanism. The project includes FPGA and VLSI implementations to demonstrate NASH performance.

🇯🇵 このプロジェクトの目的は、我々が以前開発したOASIS通信ネットワークをベースに、ハードウェアによる適応的で低消費電力のスパイクニューラルネットワークシステム（NASH）を研究・実装することです。NASHは以下の特徴を実装しています。 (1) 異なるSNNパラメータ（スパイク重み、ルーティング、隠れ層、トポロジーなど）の再構成を可能にする効率的な適応設定方法、(2) 異なる深層NNトポロジーの混合、(3) 効率的で耐障害性に優れたマルチキャストスパイクルーティングアルゴリズム、 (4) 効率的なオンチップ学習機構。NASHシステムの性能を実証するために、FPGA実装を開発し、VLSI実装も確立するものとする。

🇬🇧 Students can work on software (Python), or hardware (VLSI/FPGA) or both.

items.title: Low-power Generative Adversarial Network
items.text:
A low-power Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) is an energy-efficient version of a traditional GAN, optimized for environments with limited computational resources. By using techniques like model compression and approximate computing, it reduces energy consumption, enabling real-time data generation on low-power devices like smartphones, IoT systems, and neuromorphic hardware.

You will build a baseline GAN in PyTorch or Verilog HDL, then reduce its power consumption using our existing techniques, such as approximate computing, approximate memory, or data compression.

Students can work on software (Python), or hardware (VLSI/FPGA) or both.

items.title: Event Sensor Processing / イベントセンサ処理
items.text:
🇬🇧 This theme focuses on efficient processing of event-based sensor data. Event sensors detect changes in the environment asynchronously and generate events only when changes occur, enabling low-latency and low-power sensing.

Students will explore event data processing using AI, spiking neural networks (SNNs), FPGA, microcontrollers, and embedded systems. Possible topics include real-time object detection, event filtering and compression, hardware acceleration, and low-power event processing.

The research can cover both software algorithms and hardware implementation, with applications in robotics, edge AI, human detection, and IoT systems.

Students can work on software (Python), hardware (VLSI/FPGA), or both.

🇯🇵 本テーマでは、イベントベースセンサから得られるデータの効率的な処理について研究します。イベントセンサは環境の変化を非同期に検出し、変化が発生したときだけイベントを生成するため、低遅延・低消費電力のセンシングが可能です。

AI、スパイキングニューラルネットワーク（SNN）、FPGA、マイコン、組込みシステムなどを用いて、リアルタイム物体検出、イベントデータのフィルタリング・圧縮、ハードウェアアクセラレーション、省電力処理などを研究します。

ロボット、エッジAI、人物検出、IoTなどへの応用を目指します。

items.title: Inspiring the Next Generation: Our External Talk on Neuromorphic Computing at a Fukushima High School
items.text:
Khanh N. Dang's Point of View:

On June 28, 2023, Khanh had the exciting opportunity to give an external talk at Fukushima High School to introduce the students to the group's research on neuromorphic computing and its potential to revolutionize technology. It was a memorable experience to engage with high school students and share insights into the future of artificial intelligence (AI) and brain-inspired computing systems.

During the talk, Khanh explained the primary aspects of our research, including:

  1. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs): These brain-inspired networks are different from traditional artificial neural networks (ANNs) by mimicking the way neurons communicate with each other through electrical spikes.
  2. Chip Design: We also explore creating specialized chips, such as AI-powered chips for landslide detection, that are designed to solve real-world problems in an energy-efficient and sustainable way.
  3. How to train a silicon brain: The Hebbian learning rule is explained to help the student understand how the brain learns patterns.

The highlight of the talk was the interactive session where the students were able to ask questions and explore how neuromorphic computing could be applied to fields such as robotics, healthcare, and environmental monitoring. Khanh emphasized the importance of interdisciplinary knowledge—combining computer science, neuroscience, and engineering—to solve complex problems.

The experience was rewarding, and Khanh left feeling hopeful about the future of technology. It's always inspiring to see young minds eager to learn about the potential of AI and computing systems. Khanh looks forward to future opportunities to engage with students and continue sharing our passion for neuromorphic research.

A big thank you to Fukushima High School] for inviting me and for the warm reception. Khanh also would like to thank the Student Recruiting Section (in particular 郡司　拓哉 様) of the University of Aizu for arranging this talk. Khanh hopes the students found the talk as inspiring as Khanh did!

items.title: 1. EnsembleSTDP: Distributed In-situ Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity Learning in Spiking Neural Networks
items.text:
Authors: Yuga Hanyu and Khanh N. Dang

This paper introduces EnsembleSTDP, a distributed in-situ learning mechanism for Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs). The method leverages Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP) to enable efficient, unsupervised online learning. EnsembleSTDP enhances training speed and scalability, making it suitable for neuromorphic hardware implementations. You can read the paper here.

His travel is partially supported by the generous funding provided by the AIZU ZAIDAN fund, and we sincerely thank them for their support.

Yuga Hanyu さん, a 4th-year undergraduate student, presented this work. He has done an excellent job contributing to the research and preparing for this presentation.

items.title: 2. Energy-Efficient Spiking Neural Networks Using Approximate Neuron Circuits and 3D Stacking Memory
items.text:
Authors: Ryoji Kobayashi, Ngo-Doanh Nguyen, Nguyen Anh Vu Doan, and Khanh N. Dang

This paper proposes an energy-efficient approach to Spiking Neural Networks by combining approximate neuron circuits with 3D stacking memory. The research focuses on reducing power consumption while maintaining high performance, offering promising solutions for low-power neuromorphic computing applications. You can read the paper here.

Ryoji Kobayashi さん, also a 4th-year undergraduate student, presented this work. This is his second paper and presentation at an IEEE conference, demonstrating his growing expertise and commitment to advancing neuromorphic computing research.

items.text:
ニューラルネットワークをプロセッサに搭載する際、大量のパラメータを格納するために大きなメモリ領域が必要となり、結果として消費電力が大きくなるという課題があります。

When implementing neural networks on-chip, a large memory footprint is required to store the parameters, which leads to increased power consumption.

本研究では、これを解決するために、3Dスタック型の低消費電力ニューラルネットワークプロセッサを提案します。

To address this issue, we propose a low-power 3D-stacked neural network processor.

items.title: 1st Runner-Up and Kyushu Keisokki Co., Ltd. Award at the 29th LSI Design Contest
items.text:
News!

University News!

  • Japanese: https://u-aizu.ac.jp/information/29-lsi2026.html
  • English: https://u-aizu.ac.jp/en/information/29-lsi2026.html

We are delighted to share that our team (M1 Hanyu, M1 Atharv, and B3 Komatsuzaki) received the 1st Runner-Up Prize (Kyushu Keisokki Co., Ltd. Award) at the 29th LSI Design Contest, held in Okinawa, Japan.

The LSI Design Contest is an international competition where student teams present innovative LSI, VLSI, and hardware system designs to a panel of experts from academia and industry. The contest provides an excellent platform for students to demonstrate practical chip and system design skills, as well as creative ideas in advanced computing architectures.

In 2026, the topic of the 29th edition of the competition is Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). Over 77 participants (26 teams) from Japan and overseas applied. After the screening round, 11 teams are invited (with financial support) to present at the venue in Okinawa on March 6, 2026.

Our team presented a project on Spiking Generative Adversarial Network (Spiking GAN). The work explores how generative models can be implemented using spiking neural networks, enabling energy-efficient generative AI suitable for neuromorphic and edge computing platforms.

The project demonstrates a GAN architecture adapted to spike-based neural computation, highlighting how spiking processing can be applied to generative tasks while maintaining the efficiency advantages of neuromorphic systems.

The project was recognized for its novelty, technical contribution, and presentation quality, earning both the Runner-Up Prize and the Kyushu Keisokki Co., Ltd. Award.

We are extremely proud of the students for their hard work, dedication, and outstanding performance, representing our research group and university at this international competition.

items.title: Project Summary
items.text:
We solve the reliabilty challenges of Through-Silicon-Via based 3D Integrated Circuits with hotspot awareness. When hotspots occur, they accelerate the fault rates of their regions which lead to the need of both temporal and spatial system adaptations. Also, hotspots could be the consequences of using fault-tolerance. Therefore, we target to make the 3D-ICs not only support fault tolerance with variable fault-rates and fault distribution but also be adaptable to the occurrences of thermal hotspots.

items.title: Event Sensing
items.text: We investigate efficient processing of event-based sensor data for low-power, real-time perception. Event cameras report changes asynchronously, allowing processing to focus on activity in the scene.

items.title: Research directions
items.text:
Our research connects sensor data processing with spiking neural networks (SNNs) and embedded hardware. Topics include:

  • Event filtering and compression to reduce data movement and processing cost.
  • Real-time object and motion detection from event streams.
  • SNN processing and FPGA acceleration for low-power perception.
  • Embedded sensing systems that combine event and thermal cameras for human detection.

Students can contribute through Python software, FPGA and VLSI design, or combined hardware and software implementation. See the event sensor processing thesis theme.

items.title: Brief description
items.text:
In this research, we investigate designing a low-power neuromorphic computing solution for IoT and Edge devices by combining Approximate Computing and Approximate Stacking Memory. As IoT and edge devices have become ubiquitous, it is necessary to have the ability to calculate the neural networks on the devices using dedicated chips/modules. However, current neural network architectures are power intensive, especially for deep neural networks, which prevents them from being able to be widely adopted. As a result, there is a need for low-power solutions for Neuromorphic Computing. In this research proposal, we combine Approximate Stacking Memory with Approximate Computing to improve energy efficiency further while maintaining overall accuracy.

items.title: Information
items.text:
• Funder: KAKENHI (Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research B)
  • Project No: 26K02883
  • Duration: 2026/04-2029/03
  • Summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has made great progress, but its high energy consumption remains a serious challenge, especially for small devices such as smartphones, IoT sensors, and battery- or solar-powered systems. This project proposes a new energy-efficient neuromorphic AI accelerator using 3D integrated circuits (3D-ICs) that combine Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) and SRAM to reduce power usage both during operation and idle periods. NVM can retain data without power, significantly lowering idle energy consumption, but it is typically slower and more energy-intensive during read/write operations than SRAM. To address this, we introduce a hybrid memory architecture in which stacked NVM layers are placed above the logic layer to shorten data transfer distance, while a small, fast SRAM layer acts as a cache between logic and NVM to improve speed and reduce read/write energy. In addition, adaptive power management techniques dynamically adjust energy usage based on available power with minimal impact on accuracy and performance. With these technologies, the proposed design aims to reduce energy consumption during operation and during idle time, enabling practical low-power AI chips for real-world applications such as smartphones, IoT devices, and smart sensors.

items.title: Research Technology & Prototyping
items.text: Our research group specializes in the design and validation of high-efficiency AI hardware and next-generation memory-compute systems. We leverage industry-leading AMD (formerly Xilinx) FPGA platforms to bridge the gap between architectural theory and physical silicon realization.

items.title: Core Methodologies
items.text:
Full-System Prototyping: We utilize a rigorous RTL-based design flow (Verilog/VHDL) within the Vivado™ and Vitis™ environments. This ensures cycle-accurate hardware validation and reliable performance benchmarking for complex neural accelerators.

3D-IC & Interconnect Emulation: Recognizing the challenges of iterative 3D-IC fabrication, we use advanced Programmable Network-on-Chip (NoC) features to simulate high-bandwidth vertical interconnects and through-silicon via (TSV) latency characteristics.

Advanced Memory Modeling: Our group develops custom behavioral wrappers to model the timing, energy signatures, and data-retention properties of emerging technologies, such as Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) and high-density 3D-stacked SRAM.

By using adaptive computing platforms as high-fidelity emulation vehicles, we can explore innovative architectural trade-offs—such as Memory–Compute Co-Design and Event-Driven AI—with the precision of hardware-level execution. This methodology allows us to accelerate the development cycle for low-power AI chips targeting edge devices, smartphones, and autonomous IoT sensors.

The final program will be released in Github under MIT license in the future.
